### C-R10-01
**Claim:** Part 5c climaxes the foreign-nation messages with Babylon—the empire that fell Jerusalem—two chapters of announcements of Babylon’s fall plus associated restoration promises for Israel; the Babylon material is almost as extensive as Jer 46–49 combined, asserting Yahweh’s preeminence over the world power.
**Quote:** “With these messages about Babylon, the Jeremiah scroll comes to a climax with its assertion of the preeminence of Yahweh over the world power. … ‘This is the empire; it cannot be treated like just another nation.’”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 1–8; Jer 50–51 intro
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-02
**Claim:** Imperial readers may dislike the chapters’ “obsessional antagonism,” but revenge fantasies (imagining Yahweh’s redress) can be a survival strategy when read from the underside of empire (e.g. Kenya 1950s, Nicaragua 1980s).
**Quote:** “‘Revenge fantasies’—in this case, imagining Yahweh taking redress—can be a strategy for survival.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 8–9
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-03
**Claim:** After the Babylon material come three closings: brief conclusion pairing with 46:1 (51:58b/d), a coda of Jeremiah’s last act re Babylon (51:59–64a), and conclusion to Jeremiah’s message as a whole (51:64b).
**Quote:** “The material on Babylon is followed by a brief conclusion to the messages about other nations, pairing with the introduction to them in 46:1 (51:58b), a coda about a last act of Jeremiah in relation to Babylon (51:59–64a), and a conclusion to Jeremiah’s message as a whole (51:64b).”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 10–11; Jer 51:58–64
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-04
**Claim:** 50:1 (“The word that Yahweh spoke regarding Babylon … by means of Jeremiah the prophet”) suggests Jeremiahic origin, but Goldingay’s working assumption is adapted versions by curators: actual words of Jeremiah, supplemented words, and curator/other-prophet developments—without claiming criteria can reliably separate them.
**Quote:** “The mainstream scholarly view is that Jeremiah’s curators, too, provide adapted versions of his teaching. … I take it as my own working assumption. … I am therefore agnostic on the question of authorship, here as elsewhere … and in referring to ‘Jeremiah,’ I conflate the actual Jeremiah and whoever may be channeling him.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 12–49; Jer 50:1
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-05
**Claim:** Jer 50–51 lacks dates/historical markers of the kind in Kedar/Hazor and Elam; this raises whether Babylon becomes the ultimate enemy under nearly cosmic judgment (problem of evil; no restoration prospect like Egypt/Moab)—but Goldingay thinks cosmic-Babylon is more reception history than original sense, given concrete Medes references.
**Quote:** “Babylon’s coming to represent something beyond the historical Babylon may be more an aspect of the chapters’ reception over the centuries than part of the meaning they would have had for Jeremiah, his curators, and the people who first heard the scroll read.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 50–53; Jer 50–51; cf. Rev 18
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-06
**Claim:** Reception: fall of Babylon in 50–51 is necessary prelude to Judah’s future (30–33); Rev 18 (language richly borrowed from Jeremiah) is necessary prelude to the eternal future of Rev 21–22.
**Quote:** “‘The event so dramatically portrayed in chapters 50–51 was the necessary prelude to the historical future for Judah that had been promised in chapters 30–33. And similarly, the event portrayed in Revelation 18, in language richly borrowed from Jeremiah, is the necessary prelude to the eternal future…’”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 52–53
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-07
**Claim:** Parallel dynamic with chs. 1–20: first half names an unidentified northern aggressor before naming Babylon; 50–51 first speaks of northern aggressor against Babylon (50:3, 9, 41), only later names Medes/related peoples (51:11, 27–28). Reference only to Medes (not Persians) and to Ararat, Minni, Ashkenaz points to early/mid-sixth century, before Medo-Persian reality.
**Quote:** “Jeremiah 50–51 manifests a parallel dynamic. Initially, the chapters speak solely of an aggressor from the north who will bring Babylon’s own downfall (50:3, 9, 41); only later do they name names (51:11, 27–28).”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 54–55; Jer 1:13–15; 50–51
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-08
**Claim:** Coda 51:59–64 dates Jeremiah’s original Babylon scroll to 594; he wrote it to be thrown into the Euphrates but “all these words” that still exist imply a second copy (as with the 604 scroll). Final form of 50–51 hypothesized in 550s/540s; final dated event in the scroll is Jehoiachin’s release (562) plus “all the days of his life.”
**Quote:** “The coda to the chapters in 51:59–64 does specifically date Jeremiah’s original Babylon scroll in 594. … One might then hypothesize that the 550s or 540s are the period in which Jer 50–51 reached its final form.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 56–57; Jer 51:59–64; 52:31–34
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-09
**Claim:** Theological (not pragmatic) non-tension: 50–51’s redress on Babylon coheres with Nebuchadrezzar as Yahweh’s servant and Judah’s submission (25; 27–29)—double attitude like Isa 10:5–19 re Assyria; “yet a little while” (51:33) vs seventy years (29:10) should not be pressed. Public proclamation of 50–51 would undermine 27–29 and sound like Hananiah—supports reading the scroll as non-public (prayer/curse), for post-587 Judahite hearers.
**Quote:** “Theologically, there is no tension between Jeremiah’s urging a policy of submission to Babylon in Jer 25 and promising that Yahweh will take redress on Babylon in Jer 50–51. … It would make him sound like Hananiah.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 58–61; Jer 25; 27–29; 50–51
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-10

Arrangement not systematic (like Jer 2, 48).
**Quote:** “Behind Jeremiah’s various modes of speaking, one can perceive a number of modes of speaking from the community’s everyday life….”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 62–97
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

**Quote:** “Yahweh intends to put Babylon down himself; he assures the Judahites that imperial power and oppression will not last forever. … Given that ‘there is a time to settle and a time to flee,’ Jer 29 represented the first ‘time,’ but Judahites now need to be willing and ready to leave Babylon.”

### C-R10-27
**Claim (Seraiah colophon 51:59–64):** 594: Jeremiah orders Seraiah ben Neriah (Baruch’s brother?; accommodation official; Mahseiah scribe family) going with Zedekiah to Babylon to write entire dire fate for Babylon in one document, read it out at Babylon, address Yahweh (“you yourself spoke regarding this place”), tie stone, throw into Euphrates—“So will Babylon sink.” Dramatized fact, not bare history (many 50–51 units likely post-587, so 594 doc ≠ entire 50–51). Writing + reading + drowning = performative ensuring of fulfillment; reading is acted prayer to Yahweh (not public Jer 36-style politics). “This place” transfers from Jerusalem to Babylon. Story for post-587 readers: “Nothing can now prevent Babylon’s defeat.”
**Quote:** “This reading happens in order for Yahweh to hear it, with an implicit challenge to Yahweh to do as he has said in these messages. … Seraiah is to wave the document in Yahweh’s face. … ‘Nothing can now prevent Babylon’s defeat.’”

**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

## Epilogue (Jer 52:1–34)

### C-R10-30
**Claim (frame with ch 1):** Jer 52 frames the scroll with Jer 1; not a later addition presupposing 1–51 without it. Matches opening and whole scroll: solemn waywardness + calamity, while affirming calamity is not Yahweh’s last word. Scroll “resists closure” as aspect of disaster/trauma links.
**Quote:** “But Jer 52 forms a frame with Jer 1 around the Jeremiah scroll. With it, the scroll reaches its goal, and there is no reason to see it as a later addition, as if Jer 1–51 once existed without it. Matching the opening chapter and matching the nature of the scroll as a whole, it tells a solemn story of Judah’s waywardness and of the calamity that followed, while also affirming that calamity is not Yahweh’s last word.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2577–2582; Jer 52 // Jer 1
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-31
**Claim (function after 51:64b):** Answers “What happened, then? Did those words of Jeremiah come true?” without naming Jeremiah: fulfillment both horrible and encouraging. Vindicates Jeremiah as true prophet while showing human mediation’s ineffectiveness to prevent disaster. “Pull up, pull down, wipe out, smash: ‘Never were four words more fully realized.’”
**Quote:** “Following on 51:64b, it answers the question, ‘What happened, then? Did those words of Jeremiah come true?’ … The answer it implies is that Jeremiah’s words indeed found some measure of fulfillment, both horribly and encouragingly.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2582–2582
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-32
**Claim (calamity short of annihilation / hope short of full renewal):** Balance reflects Jeremiah’s message: much waywardness, much trouble, but a glimmer of hope. Both calamity and reestablishment fall short of Yahweh’s threats and promises (usual pattern). No actual annihilation and no genuine full renewal; frightful calamity + hint of extraordinary restoration; something, not nothing. Hope notes: some left as vinedressers/tillers; tiny deportation numbers; fighters scattered (not all dead); temple bronze/accoutrements to Babylon but not “lost”; Jehoiachin released.
**Quote:** “The story forms an apposite closure for the scroll insofar as its balance reflects that of Jeremiah’s message: much waywardness, much consequential trouble, but a glimmer of hope. Both calamity and reestablishment fall way short of Yahweh’s threats and promises, in keeping with the usual pattern. There was no actual annihilation and no genuine renewal. There was frightful calamity but also a hint of extraordinary restoration. There was something, not nothing.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2582–2584
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-33
**Claim (text-critical/source situation):** MT and LXX agree 52 closes the scroll; mostly // 2 Kgs 24:18–25:30; overlaps Jer 37–43 / 39:1–10. Distinctive MT Jer 52: no Gedaliah, includes deportation numbers, no Cyrus commission (which Chronicles sees as fulfilling Jeremiah). No mention of Jeremiah’s fate or vindication by name. Like 50–51, hardly postdates 539; 550s/540s fit with vv. 31–34.
**Quote:** “The most noticeable distinctive features of Jer 52 MT are its lack of reference to Gedaliah, its inclusion of the numbers of Judahites taken to Babylon, and its lack of reference to Cyrus’s commission…. Like Jer 50–51, it hardly postdates 539; in light of vv. 31–34, a date in the 550s or 540s makes sense.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2691–2696
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-34
**Claim (52:1–3):** Opens with Zedekiah’s accession (not rebellion alone)—Babylon installed him expecting subordination (= Jeremiah’s exhortation). Double irony of renaming Mattaniah → Zedekiah (“Yah my faithfulness”): he did not live up to the name. MT only: did dire like Jehoiakim; “because it was directed toward Yahweh’s anger… until he threw them out.” Scroll juxtaposes Yahweh-anger perspective and power-politics perspective without reducing to either.
**Quote:** “In this situation the prophet saw that another opportunity had been given by God to the people…. But Zedekiah did not live up to his name.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2697–2702; Jer 52:1–3
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-35
**Claim (52:3b–16 fall narrative):** Rebellion → 18-month siege (not continuous; cf. 37:5); city “broke open,” men of battle flee, Zedekiah caught Jericho steppes; sons slaughtered before eyes (line ends—contrast Jehoiachin); eyes blinded; house of custody until death (// contrast v. 34). Month later: Nebuzaradan burns temple, palace, houses; pulls down walls; exiles some poor/remaining; leaves some as vinedressers and farmworkers—first hope note in a series.
**Quote:** “Their position is less explicit here than it was at 39:10…. That earlier account makes clearer that it is for their own sake that they are tending vines… but the repetition in v. 16 over against v. 15 suggests that this note is the first of a series of notes of hope running through the chapter.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2703–2708; Jer 52:3b–16
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-36
**Claim (52:17–27 temple + leaders):** Catalog of temple bronze/gold/silver vessels witnesses community pain (// 1 Kgs 7; longer than 2 Chr 36:19 because earlier, pre-rebuild). Likely conflates 597 and 587 pillagings. Seraiah head priest (≠ 51:59 Seraiah), Zephaniah, threshold keepers, military/elite arrested and executed at Riblah. “So Judah went into exile from upon its land.”
**Quote:** “The lists of temple articles and the account of what happened to them witness to the pain of the community that watched them be destroyed or stolen.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2710–2711; Jer 52:17–27
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-37
**Claim (52:28–30 deportation numbers):** Unique list: 597 → 3,023; 587 → 832; 582 → 745; total 4,600. Small numbers vs 2 Kgs 24 figures (maybe men only). Significance: Yahweh’s action softer than threats; 587 not beginning of exile (597 more significant break); 582 only here (guess: reprisal for Jer 41). Supports empty-land-as-myth; land not emptied. Multiple Judahite communities/voices post-587 (Judah, Egypt, Babylon) with differing views—scroll speaks with more than one voice (24 bad figs vs 40 less gloomy; 44 threatens Egypt but community flourished).
**Quote:** “They indicate that as usual, Yahweh’s action is softer than his threats. … The small numbers support the notion that the myth of an empty land is indeed a myth—the land was by no means emptied.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2712–2715; Jer 52:28–30
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-38
**Claim (Jehoiachin release 52:31–34 — glimmer of hope):** Thirty-seventh year of Jehoiachin’s exile: Evil-merodach (Amel-Marduk; Heb. ʾĕwîl-mәrōdak may pun “fool of Marduk”) lifts Jehoiachin’s head from confinement, speaks good things, sets throne above other captive kings, regular table and provision until day of death, all days of life. Unexpected vs 22:24–30 (no change of heart indicated). Sign Yahweh may not be finished with Judah and David’s line; grandson Zerubbabel later leads (Ezra 3) though not as king. Dating by Jehoiachin’s exile (not Babylonian king) is itself suggestive. Contrast Zedekiah custody-until-death vs Jehoiachin reestablished-until-death. Babylonian oil tablets already call him “king of Judah” under Nebuchadrezzar. Chronicles omits this elevation and instead uses Cyrus stirring (Jeremiah fulfillment)—more hindsight; Jer 52 pre-539.
**Quote:** “What we do get is a final hopeful coda to the story. … ‘the sense of an ending offered by ch. 52 is also tinged with the sense of a new beginning.’ … It is a sign that Yahweh may not be finished with Judah and specifically with the line of David.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2716–2725; Jer 52:31–34
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]

### C-R10-39
**Claim (closing pastoral/theological synthesis of epilogue):** Anyone leaving during the “credits” misses the vital encouragement. Closing Calvin prayer: fruit of Jeremiah’s labors for later ages; devote to God’s service and kingdom of the Son until celestial rest.
**Quote:** “So anyone yielding to the temptation to leave the movie theater during the credits would miss something vital and encouraging.”
**Locus:** Slice ll. 2584; 2727–2732
**Targets:** [[jeremiah]], [[john-goldingay]], [[goldingay-jeremiah-nicot]]
